analysis.one_liner: Repeals tax credits that pay oil companies to inject carbon dioxide into wells to pump more oil.
analysis.headline: The bill died without a vote: it was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and the committee never acted on it before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal tax law currently pays companies to capture carbon dioxide and inject it into old oil fields to squeeze out more oil — and separately gives a tax credit for enhanced oil recovery itself. This bill would end both: it removes the credit for using carbon dioxide as a drilling aid for new facilities and repeals the enhanced oil recovery credit entirely. It never got a committee hearing or a floor vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary taxpayers, who currently fund these credits, and anyone who wants federal dollars stopped from subsidizing oil production. The bill's changes take effect for tax years after enactment, so savings would build over time.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals section 43 of the tax code, the existing tax credit for enhanced oil recovery, effective for tax years after enactment.

It blocks a separate carbon capture credit from paying companies that use captured carbon dioxide as a 'tertiary injectant' — an agent pumped into wells to force out more oil — for facilities whose construction begins after enactment.
It was introduced by Rep. Ro Khanna with 18 Democratic cosponsors.

analysis.who_pays: Oil companies that use carbon dioxide flooding to boost production, and the carbon capture and industrial gas firms that supply them, would lose federal tax subsidies. Removing the subsidies could modestly reduce production at fields that depend on the credits.

drawbacks.text: The carbon dioxide used for enhanced oil recovery is injected underground and some of it stays there, so the same credit the bill ends has been argued to support some carbon retention as well as more drilling; the bill would remove that incentive for new projects.

The bill does not touch the carbon capture credit for existing facilities already under construction, so companies with projects underway would keep collecting subsidies for carbon dioxide used in oil recovery.
Ending the credits could slightly reduce domestic oil output at fields that rely on carbon dioxide flooding.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would save taxpayers money by ending subsidies to a mature, profitable industry, and the environmental case is straightforward: paying companies to produce more oil under a 'carbon capture' label is hard to defend. The honest costs are modest — some oil fields that depend on these credits could scale back, and the grandfathering for existing carbon capture projects means the taxpayer subsidies the bill targets would phase out only slowly for projects already built.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never scheduled any action on it, and it died when the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Ro Khanna introduced the bill on September 25, 2024, joined by 18 Democratic cosponsors including Ms. Norton, Ms. Tlaib, Mr. Raskin, and Ms. Ocasio-Cortez.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, which holds jurisdiction over tax legislation.
The action history shows no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor action after the referral.
The 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025, and the bill received no further action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil companies that use carbon dioxide to pump more oil keep their federal tax credits, and taxpayers keep paying for them. A bill with zero Republican cosponsors and no committee action had no realistic path in this Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil producers keeping their tax credits

for.name: Rep. Ro Khanna
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to end tax credits for carbon dioxide used in oil recovery.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Jason Smith (R-MO)
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral — no hearing, no markup, no committee vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 19 supporters (the sponsor and 18 cosponsors) were House Democrats, and the committee that buried it was controlled by Republicans with no Republican cosponsor anywhere.

industries.industry: Oil producers using CO2 enhanced recovery
industries.note: These companies collect a dedicated tax credit (section 43) plus carbon capture credits (section 45Q) for injecting carbon dioxide to force more oil out of wells. The bill would end that public funding; its defeat means the credits continue.

industries.industry: Carbon capture and industrial gas suppliers
industries.note: Firms that capture CO2 and sell it to oil fields for enhanced recovery would lose the 45Q credit for new projects under the bill. Existing projects are grandfathered, so current revenue streams would be largely protected.
